Big Five self-reports become more coherent and differentiated with age, but the magnitude and pattern of these age effects differ for the different personality domains, and these patterns are not simply due to changes in verbal comprehension.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Big Five personality traits of children and adolescents are not the same as the Big Five personality characteristics of adults.
the Big Five personality traits show different developmental patterns, and these patterns are related to the psychometrics of the self-reports.
personality development is a complex process, which is not linear and not the same for every individual.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Big Five personality structure is present at age 10, but it is not yet fully formed.
the development of personality traits from late childhood through early adulthood is complex and domain specific.
the developmental trends in personality self-reports are not uniform, and the nature of the developmental trends depends on the specific Big Five domain.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Big Five is a useful tool for studying personality in childhood and adolescence, but it is important to recognize that the Big Five has a somewhat different structure at younger ages, and that this developmental change has important implications for the interpretation of findings.
